list.listitem: In the absence of "red flag" symptoms, clinicians should not routinely order imaging or other diagnostic tests in patients with nonspecific low back pain (LBP). A

Imaging after a trial of therapy is recommended for patients with signs or symptoms of radiculopathy; risk factors or symptoms of spinal stenosis; or minor risk factors for cancer, inflammatory back disease, and/or vertebral compression fracture. Prolonged conservative therapy is an option for appropriate patients who wish to avoid surgery. B
Back exercises with education appear effective at preventing an episode of back pain and are more effective than lumbar support or back school in secondary prevention. B

Patients with nonspecific acute LBP without sciatica should be managed conservatively beginning with nondrug therapies including heat, massage, acupuncture, and/or spinal manipulation and advice to stay active. B NSAIDs or skeletal muscle relaxants can be used for pain; combinations of drugs do not appear to be superior to monotherapy, and acetaminophen appears to be ineffective for acute LBP. A Bed rest should be avoided. A
Spinal manipulation is no better or worse than other treatments for acute LBP. A

background.definition: Acute LBP is pain, muscle tension, or stiffness localized posteriorly between the lower rib cage and the inferior gluteal folds that is less than 6 weeks in duration.

list.listitem: The incidence of LBP in the adult general population is between 14% and 23% per year.
Most episodes are mild. Only 1% develops intense LBP. Complete resolution occurs in 27% to 29%, and approximately 30% have a recurrence within 6 months.

LBP lasting at least 1 day in the past 3 months was reported by 29% of U.S. adults in the 2010 National Health Interview Survey. Asian Americans had the lowest prevalence (18.5%) and prevalence declined with higher education and income.
The mean point prevalence in 10 studies of children and adolescents was 0.120 (95% CI, 0.09-0.159).
Among hospital physicians, the annual prevalence of LBP was 33% to 68%.

Among patients presenting with LBP to the emergency department (ED), authors of a meta-analysis of 22 studies with 41,320 patients found a prevalence of serious spinal pathology requiring immediate/urgent treatment of 2.5% to 5.1% in prospective and 0.7% to 7.4% in retrospective studies. Identified disorders included 0% to 7.2% for vertebral fractures, 0% to 2.1% for spinal cancer, 0% to 1.9% for infectious disorders, 0.1% to 1.9% for pathologies with spinal cord/cauda equina compression, and 0% to 0.9% for vascular pathologies.
Over $90 billion is spent on health care for back pain. Additionally, back pain accounts for 33% of all worker's compensation costs.

Annual medical cost for patients with spine problems was $4695 between 1997 and 2005, compared with $2731 among those without spine problems. In 2005, the expenditures among adults with spine problems increased 65%, more rapidly than overall health expenditures.
In a recent systematic review, among community-dwelling adults, the prevalence of back pain in the past 3 months was 33.9% and these patients contributed $365 billion in all-cause medical costs.
LBP was the tenth most common reason for medical office visits in the U.S. in the 2012 National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NAMCS), and is a leading cause of work-related disability.
In 2018, LBP was the diagnosis for 4,599,000 visits in ambulatory care which represented 0.5% distribution of office visits based on data from NAMCS.
Acute LBP of nonspecific musculoskeletal origin (muscle strain) accounts for more than 85% of cases.
About 1% of patients with acute LBP in the primary care setting have a serious underlying cause.

In a prospective cohort study of 669 patients aged 55 years and older with back pain consulting their GP, 6% were diagnosed with serious underlying pathology during the 1-year follow-up. Most of these participants (5%) were diagnosed with a vertebral fracture.
Most patients with acute back pain have no clear or identifiable underlying pathology.

Some patients have specific underlying causes for their pain: fracture (4%), tumor (0.7%), rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis or other autoimmune arthropathies (0.3%), or infection (0.01%). In a Cochrane review of eight trials of patients presenting with LBP, vertebral fracture was responsible for 0.7% to 4.5% of cases in primary care settings.
Hyperalgesia and spinal cord hyperexcitability have been detected in initial stages of nonspecific LBP, although it is unclear if these are widespread effects.
Vitamin D receptor gene polymorphisms are associated with risk of intervertebral disc degeneration in Caucasians.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: High television viewing time (≥2 hours/day for women with low disability)
Psychological factors such as depression or anxiety

list.listitem: There is conflicting evidence about the benefit of exercise interventions to prevent LBP, although exercise should be encouraged for its other health benefits. B In a cluster RCT performed with 708 children aged 8 to 11 years, children who were taught four spinal movements for daily practice in addition to education on "back awareness” had significantly fewer episodes of LBP (OR 0.54; 95% CI, 0.39-0.74) and significantly fewer lifetime first episodes of LBP evaluated at about 8½ months compared with the control group receiving education only (34% vs. 47%).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that moderate-quality evidence supports use of exercise combined with education to reduce the risk of an episode of LBP (RR 0.55; 95% CI, 0.41-0.74) but not sick leave (low-quality evidence).

Lumbar supports or back belts are ineffective in preventing LBP. A Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that manual material-handling advice and training (with or without assistive devices) does not prevent back pain or back pain-related disability. High-quality studies are needed. B Use of customized orthotic insoles also do not appear effective.
Back exercises are more effective than lumbar support or back school in secondary prevention; a Cochrane review also supported use of exercise to prevent recurrences of back pain. B
There is some evidence to support the "Alexander technique" for posture training. B
Clinicians should not routinely order imaging; randomized trials do not show clinical benefit of routine imaging over usual care in patients without indications. B
Immediate radiography plus ESR is recommended in patients with major risk factors of cancer (see Imaging). B
Immediate MRI is recommended in patients with risk factors for spinal infection or risk factors for or signs of cauda equina syndrome or severe or progressive neurologic deficits (see Imaging). B

Imaging after a trial of therapy is recommended in patients with signs or symptoms of radiculopathy; risk factors or symptoms of spinal stenosis; or minor risk factors for: cancer, inflammatory back disease, or vertebral compression fracture. B
Repeated imaging is only recommended for patients with new or changed low-back symptoms. B

list.listitem: The primary goal of the detailed history and physical examination is to rule out serious conditions requiring more extensive work-up or immediate surgical evaluation. "Red flags" in the history associated with cancer are: age over 50 years, history of cancer, or unexplained weight loss. However, there is limited supporting evidence for the usefulness of these factors, except for prior cancer, for detecting spinal malignancy. A history of prior cancer predicts cancer in 1 in 14 patients with acute LBP in primary care and 1 in 3 patients presenting to an emergency department.

In a meta-analysis of 22 studies of patients presenting with LBP to the ED, red flags that increased the likelihood for a serious condition were suspicion or history of cancer (for spinal cancer), intravenous (IV) drug use, indwelling vascular catheter, and other infection site (for epidural abscess).

Authors of a retrospective study of 1000 consecutive patients presenting to the ED with LBP, of whom 3.3% had serious spinal and 14.6% had serious non-spinal pathologies, red flags for any serious condition included fever (LR+ 68.8), tuberculosis history (LR+ 13.8), known nephrolithiasis/abdominal aortic aneurysm (LR+ 10.2), unexplained weight-loss (LR+ 9.2), writhing in pain (LR+ 6.9), urinary symptoms (LR+ 5.4), and flank pain (LR+ 5.2). Red flags for serious spinal pathology included saddle anesthesia (LR+ 11.0), tuberculosis history (LR+ 9.8), IV drug use (LR+ 6.9), acute-onset urinary retention (LR+ 6.4), and anal tone loss (LR+ 6.3).

Other symptoms suggestive of serious underlying pathology are: fever or chills, significant trauma, osteoporosis, unrelenting night pain, progressive motor or sensory deficit, saddle anesthesia, bowel or bladder incontinence, or immunosuppression.

Red flags for vertebral fracture were also of limited usefulness in another Cochrane descriptive review. Only three factors were useful although imprecise—significant trauma, older age, and corticosteroid use. LR+ point estimates ranged from 3.42 to 12.85, 3.69 to 9.39, 3.97 to 48.50 respectively. Combining red flags was more informative. These three risk factors in addition to presence of a contusion or abrasion were associated with increased likelihood of fracture in patients with LBP in a more recent systematic review.

listitem.strong: Nerve root compression and disc herniation

list.listitem: In a case series of 200 patients undergoing EMG in an academic center for suspected cervical or lumbosacral root compression, dermatomal pain was the most sensitive and segmental reflex loss and myotomal weakness were the most specific individual predictors of nerve root disease.

Overall, the history and physical examination are not terribly accurate, although most data arise from surgical populations. The single best element of the history and physical examination to exclude herniated disc is absence of sciatica. Simple office-based tests with modest accuracy for herniated disc include straight leg raise, crossed straight leg raise, and testing the strength and reflexes of lower extremities.

In one retrospective chart review study of patients with a definitive diagnosis for their LBP (based on provocation diskography or facet joint [FJ] or sacroiliac joint [SIJ] blocks), the presence of midline LBP increased the probability of lumbar disk disease and reduced the probability of symptomatic FJ and SIJ dysfunction, while the presence of paramidline LBP increased the probability of symptomatic FJ or SIJ dysfunction.

Elements in the history or physical examination with the highest likelihood ratios for spinal stenosis in patients with back or leg pain are wide-based gait (LR+ 14.3), urinary disturbance (LR+ 7.0) improvement in pain when bending over (LR+ 6.5), no pain when seated (LR+ 6.6) and perineal numbness (LR+ 5.0).

See chapter on chronic back pain for a more detailed discussion of diagnosis for chronic conditions. Specific elements that best evaluate for the presence or absence of specific diagnoses include decreased spine flexion or chest expansion (ankylosing spondylitis),spinal tenderness to percussion (osteomyelitis), wide based gait and no or improved symptoms when seated (spinal stenosis), and history of cancer (cancer).

Rapid or routine MRI early in the care of patients increases cost, mainly from increased lumbar spine surgeries, without significantly improving pain or long-term function. Among asymptomatic adult volunteers, 17% have disk herniation on MRI. Over 80% of people over 80 years of age have disk degeneration.

Therefore, clinicians should not routinely order imaging or other diagnostic tests in patients with nonspecific LBP. In the absence of "red flag" symptoms, patients should be treated conservatively for 6 weeks before considering imaging.

Interventions that can reduce imaging for patients presenting with acute LBP include clinical decision support in a hospital setting and targeted reminders to primary care physicians. In a cluster-randomized trial of 418 patients with LBP, patients who received a booklet containing information on use of inappropriate imaging given to them by practitioners who received a 30-minute training session on the booklet’s use, reduced the proportion of patients who underwent imaging examinations over 12 months compared to the control group (OR 0.50, 95%Cl 0.30 to 0.83). There were no differences in other outcomes measures including physical function or sick leave.

Immediate imaging (radiography plus ESR) is recommended in patients with major risk factors for cancer (new onset pain with history of cancer, multiple risk factors for cancer, or strong clinical suspicion of cancer).

Immediate imaging with MRI is recommended in patients with risk factors for spinal infection (new onset of LBP with fever, history of intravenous drug use, recent infection) or risk factors for or signs of cauda equina syndrome (new urinary retention, fecal incontinence, saddle anesthesia) or severe or progressive neurologic deficits (progressive motor weakness or motor deficits at multiple neurologic levels).

Imaging after a trial of therapy is recommended in patients with signs or symptoms of radiculopathy; risk factors or symptoms of spinal stenosis; or minor risk factors for cancer, inflammatory back disease, or vertebral compression fracture. Inflammatory back disease should be considered in acute LBP presenting in childhood, late adolescence, or early adulthood.

Plain radiography is recommended after a trial of therapy for: possible vertebral compression fracture in high-risk patients (eg, >65 years of age for men or >75 years for women, history of osteoporosis, steroid use, significant trauma); patients with weak risk factors for cancer (eg, age >50 years, or unexplained weight loss); or patients with risk factors or signs of ankylosing spondylitis (age 20-40 years, morning stiffness that improves with exercise, alternating buttock pain, awakening because of back pain during the latter part of the night).

MRI is the preferred imaging study for patients who are candidates for surgery or epidural steroid injection with persistent LBP and signs of radiculopathy (back pain with leg pain in an L4, L5, or S1 nerve root distribution or positive results on SLR or crossed SLR test) or surgical candidates with risk factors or symptoms of spinal stenosis.

The initial goal is to determine whether the LBP is nonspecific, with or without radiculopathy, and to identify patients with symptoms suggestive of serious underlying conditions, such as cauda equina, tumor, fracture, or infection (see ).
Because psychological factors have important prognostic value, they should be assessed at the beginning of an episode of acute LBP.
There is insufficient evidence for contribution of placebo effects to treatment for acute and subacute LBP, although placebo effects can influence chronic LBP intensity and disability.

Keep pregnancy- and lactation-associated osteoporosis (PLO) in mind for women presenting with low back pain during pregnancy or breastfeeding. The incidence of PLO is low, but likely underreported. PLO can lead to compression fractures in vertebrae and disabling back pain.

Patients with nonspecific acute LBP without sciatica should be managed conservatively with pain control with heat, topical or oral NSAIDs or other analgesics, and advice to stay active and/or exercise. Bed rest and opioids should be avoided. A Combining drugs does not appear to increase effectiveness, with the possible exception of B vitamins. A
Oral corticosteroids do not improve acute LBP and carry rare but potentially serious harms.

The American College of Physicians (ACP, 2017) guidelines recommend starting with nondrug approaches for patients with acute LBP including heat (moderate-quality evidence), massage, acupuncture, or spinal manipulation (low-quality evidence). B

The most recent ACP systematic review only identified acupuncture as effective non-drug treatment for acute LBP. NSAIDS and muscle relaxants were also found to be effective, with mild to moderate short-term benefit, for acute LBP.
Even with severe sciatica at 6 to 12 weeks, conservative therapy without surgery is successful for many if neurologic symptoms do not occur.

Spinal manipulation does not appear to be better than other treatments for acute LBP; patients with symptoms <2 weeks, no symptoms below the knee, or having back-related leg pain are most likely to benefit. A
There is insufficient evidence to recommend herbs or massage for acute LBP, although authors of a recent systematic review found acupuncture to be modestly effective for acute LBP. B
Medications with evidence of short-term pain relief for patients with acute LBP include NSAIDs and skeletal muscle relaxants.

Based on an updated Cochrane review of 32 trials with 5356 participants with acute LBP, there is moderate-quality evidence that NSAIDs are slightly more effective in short-term (≤3 weeks) reduction of pain intensity than placebo (mean difference [MD] -7.29, 95% CI, -10.98 to -3.61; 4 RCTs with 815 patients) and high-quality evidence that NSAIDs are slightly more effective for short-term improvement in disability (MD -2.02, 95% CI, -2.89 to -1.15; 2 RCTs with 471 patients). However, the magnitude of benefit is small and may not be clinically relevant. There were no differences between groups for adverse effects.

In a recent 3-arm RCT comparing a 5-day supply of 600 mg of ibuprofen, 10 mg of ketorolac, or 50 mg of diclofenac, used every 8 hours as needed for 198 patients (of 868 patients screened) with acute musculoskeletal LBP seen in the ED, no important differences between groups were found in improvement in the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire. Stomach irritation was reported in 16 of 62 (26%) on ibuprofen vs. three of 61 (5%) in the ketorolac arm and six of 64 (9%) in the diclofenac arm.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 24 trials on acute LBP found muscle relaxants to be effective for non-specific LBP, but the adverse effects, especially central nervous system adverse effects, require that they be used with caution. Authors of a more recent systematic review and meta-analysis of muscle relaxants for non-specific LBP, including 31 trials with 6505 participants, confirmed a reduction in pain intensity compared with control groups at 2 weeks or less, based on very-low-certainty evidence, with a likely increase in the risk of an adverse event.
Tolperisone, a nonopioid, centrally-acting muscle relaxant, is undergoing development for use in acute, painful back muscles spasms.

With respect to acetaminophen, authors of a Cochrane review of high-quality evidence from two trials with 1785 subjects found that paracetamol 4 g daily was ineffective for reducing pain intensity or disability, or for improving quality of life in the short term in people with acute LBP. In addition, there was no difference in recovery time for patients randomized to regular or as-needed paracetamol compared with placebo in a RCT of 1652 patients with acute LBP.

Evidence is limited for evaluating antiseizure medications for acute LBP. For patients with acute or chronic sciatica, pregabalin was no more effective than placebo for reducing leg pain at either 8 or 52 weeks. Based on two meta-analyses of 9 and 8 RCTs, respectively, neither gabapentin nor pregabalin are effective for patients with LBP with or without radiculopathy; these drugs are associated with an increased risk for adverse events.

There is little evidence supporting opioid use in acute LBP, but strong opioids for short-term use can be considered for patients with severe pain. Opioids efficacy for acute LBP is inferred from studies of other types of pain and opioids do not appear to expedite return to work in injured workers or improve functional outcomes of acute back pain in primary care. Authors of a systematic review of 14 studies at high-risk of bias found that opioids were superior to placebo for acute LBP but were not superior to other medications.

No studies were found evaluating the use of oral or epidural corticosteroids in acute LBP without sciatica. Three small studies found that systemic steroids provide no clinically significant benefit compared with placebo in acute LBP with sciatica.
Acetaminophen plus ibuprofen was not found to be more effective than ibuprofen alone at 1 week in an RCT of 120 patients presenting to the ED with acute non-traumatic, non-radicular LBP.

Similarly, in an RCT of 240 patients (31 lost to follow-up) with acute LBP, there were no differences in pain or functional improvement with the addition of acetaminophen or magnesium to an NSAID at 10 days, although at day 4, the magnesium plus NSAID group showed greater improvement than the other 2 groups.

In an RCT of 240 patients presenting to the emergency department with acute non-traumatic, nonradicular LBP, combination naproxen+orphenadrine (an antihistamine) or naproxen+methocarbamol (a muscle relaxant) was no better than naproxen alone for disability at 1 week. Reporting of adverse events was similar between groups at 9%, 19% and 17%, respectively.

In another RCT by these investigators including 320 patients presenting to the ED with non-radicular LBP of 2 weeks' duration or less, there was no difference in improvement in disability scores at 1 week using 600 mg of ibuprofen up to 3 times daily alone or with baclofen 10 mg, metaxalone 400 mg, or tizanidine 2 mg (taken as 1 or 2 capsules up to 3 times a day, as needed). All groups improved.
The addition of diazepam to naproxen did not improve disability or pain scores in patients with acute LBP in one RCT.

In an RCT of patients with acute, nontraumatic, nonradicular LBP presenting to the ED, adding cyclobenzaprine or oxycodone/acetaminophen to naproxen alone did not improve functional outcomes or pain at 1 week or 3 months.

Combination diclofenac plus B vitamins thiamine, pyridoxine, and cyanocobalamin was associated with a significant reduction in treatment duration for acute LBP compared to diclofenac monotherapy (OR 2.23; 95% CI, 1.59-3.13, 4 studies, 1108 patients).

The quality of studies of injection therapy is poor, and most fail to show any benefit in patients with LBP. In a small RCT of 50 patients with acute lumbosacral radicular syndrome, a single steroid injection with 80 mg of triamcinolone led to a small but significant improvement in the physical domains of the Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short-Form Health Survey at some of the time points. Both groups experienced a significant increase in quality of life by 4 weeks.

In a meta-analysis of six studies of 701 patients with radicular low back pain or spinal stenosis of any duration, steroid injection was not clinically different from placebo treatment with respect to pain and function at short-term (2 weeks to 3 months) or intermediate-term (3 months to 1 year) follow-up. There was no effect on symptoms of spinal stenosis. National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) guideline recommends against use of injections of anything into the back.

In an RCT of 60 patients with lumbar facet joint pain, pain-severity scores decreased at 2 weeks, and 1, 3, and 6 months after either intraarticular steroid injection or lumbar facet joint pulsed radiofrequency treatment, with about half of patients reporting successful pain relief at 6 months. Corticosteroid injections were significantly better than pulsed radiofrequency in reducing pain at the 2-week and 1-month posttreatment assessment.

In a study of acute and subacute LBP, use of either locally-injectable collagen 4 ml or trimecaine 1% 4 ml given as subcutaneous paravertebral injections into eight pre-specified points twice weekly for 2 weeks and then once in the third week resulted in a statistically significant improvement in mobility and quality of life in both groups with less use of rescue medication in patients treated with collagen.

Mesotherapy is a series of small intradermal or subcutaneous injections of various substances such as vitamins, plant extracts, pharmaceuticals and hormones. In an RCT of 120 adults presenting to the ED with acute LBP and a positive straight-leg raising test related to MRI-proven disk herniation, mesotherapy (50 or more injections of a muscle relaxant thiocolchicoside, lidocaine and the NSAID tenoxicam in selected areas from L1 to S1) compared to IV dexketoprofen decreased pain intensity at 15, 30 and 60 minutes and at 24 hours, and reduced the need for analgesics at 24 hours.
American Pain Society Guidelines recommend against facet joint injection, prolotherapy, or intradiscal steroids for patients with persistent nonradicular LBP.

A study set in the ED with patients who had low back pain of uncertain chronicity, adding an intradermal sterile water injection reduced pain, reduced opioid use, and increased patient satisfaction likely due to provoking a strong placebo response.

In an RCT of 283 patients with severe sciatica, 60% of those randomized to 6 to 12 weeks of conservative therapy did not require surgery and outcomes at 1 year were similar between conservative therapy and the surgical group.

Discectomy is effective for carefully selected patients with LBP with sciatica and disk herniation who fail to improve with conservative therapy. Diskectomy increases self-reported improvement compared with physiotherapy at 1 year (NNT 3) but not in 4 or 10 years. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis, however, found no clinically relevant benefit on pain, functioning, or quality of life from surgery for lumbar disc herniation.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 14 studies comparing outcomes of percutaneous endoscopic lumbar discectomy vs. other surgeries for patients with lumbar disc herniation found shorter operative time and hospital stays with similar success rates and complication rates; however, discectomy was associated with a significantly higher rate of recurrent disc herniation (RR 1.65; 95% CI, 1.08-2.52).

No statistically significant difference in disability score or pain at 18 weeks was found between microdiscectomy or transforaminal epidural steroid injection in an RCT including 163 patients with sciatica due to prolapsed intervertebral disc with <1 year symptom duration.

For patients with burst fracture of the thoracolumbar and lumbar spine, one RCT of 46 patients found comparable long-term results for short segmental fixation with or without fusion with respect to kyphotic angle and functional outcomes. Regional segmental motion was preserved in the non-fusion group, although more patients in this group underwent additional surgery to remove implants.
For patients with spinal stenosis, authors of the meta-analysis noted above, found a clinically relevant effect on pain and function from surgery.

For patients with spinal stenosis or chronic low back pain, there is little benefit for lumbar fusion and risk of reoperation is greater than for patients undergoing surgical decompression alone (RR 1.17; 95% CI, 1.06-1.28). However, lumbar fusion for patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis appears to be beneficial.

However, authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCT investigating surgery for lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis, including 275 patients in the decompression group and 375 in the fusion group, found no statistic differences in pain, disability scores, postoperative complications, secondary operation, or postoperative degenerative spondylolisthesis with between groups.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies with 29,066 patients also found no benefit of combining fusion with decompression in patients with lumbar spinal stenosis. In this study, reoperation rates were not significantly different between groups.

Sequestrectomy, removal of only the free fragment or sequester without clearing the intervertebral disc space, may perform as well as conventional microdiscectomy for lumbar disc herniation with respect to pain and re-herniation, although there are no RCTs comparing these approaches.
The weight of evidence is against vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty (injection of polymethylmethacrylate into fractured vertebral bodies) for osteoporotic acute vertebral compression fractures.

Several trials evaluated the effectiveness of herbal medications in nonspecific LBP. Evidence for pain reduction over placebo was strongest for Capsicum frutescens (cayenne; cream). Harpagophytum procumbens (Devil's claw; oral), Salix alba (white willow bark; oral), S. officinale L. (comfrey; nonoral), S. chinensis (nonoral), and lavender essential oil. All seem to reduce pain more than placebo, but evidence for these substances was of moderate quality at best. There is no evidence that these substances are safe or effective for long-term use.

Tibetan traditional medicine CheeZheng Pain-Relieving Plaster was associated with improved acute LBP outcomes compared to diclofenac based on a meta-analysis of 9 trials moderate to high risk of bias including 1674 patients.
Authors of a systematic review found that glucosamine was not effective for treatment of lumbar osteoarthritis.

Single-dose oral cannabidiol (400 mg CBD), as an adjunct to standard care, was not effective for relieving acute back pain at 2 hours after administration in the emergency department in an RCT with 100 participants.

In multiple RCTs, spinal manipulative therapy was slightly better than sham therapy (10 mm difference on a 100 mm visual analogue scale, 95% CI, 2-17 mm). However, manipulation does not appear to be better than other treatments. Authors of a systemic review and meta-analysis showed spinal manipulative therapy was associated with modest improvement in pain and function up to 6 weeks with transient musculoskeletal harms (increased pain, muscle stiffness, headache). NICE endorses manual therapy as a treatment option.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 trials including 2019 participants with acute or chronic back pain, however, found no clinically-relevant differences between manual therapy and sham therapy based on very low-quality evidence.

Patients with symptoms for less than 16 days and who have no symptoms extending below the knee are more likely to benefit from spinal manipulation. Similarly, among patients with non-specific LBP, manual therapy was effective for pain reduction at intermediate-term follow-up (standardized mean difference -0.72; 95% CI -1.40 to -0.04).

Authors of a recent meta-analysis of 15 RCTs with 1117 patients with acute LBP found spinal manipulation had a statistically significant association with improvements in pain over sham or alternative treatments at 6 weeks.

In an RCT of 192 patients with back-related leg pain with or without neurologic signs, more patients randomized to chiropractic spinal manipulation achieved at least a 50% reduction in pain at 3 months compared to those receiving intense home exercise and advice alone (60% vs. 44%; NNT 6.3; 95% CI, 3.4-62.5). However, there was no difference between groups at 1 year.
There is some evidence from a Cochrane review that combined chiropractic interventions produce modest benefit in short term pain and disability.

The data on the effectiveness of acupuncture for acute LBP are mixed. In a recent systematic review of 11 acute LBP RCTs, acupuncture appeared more effective for improving symptoms than NSAIDs but results were inconsistent for pain relief over medications. Acupuncture was more effective in relieving pain than sham acupuncture in two studies but did not influence function or disability. In the most recent systematic review for the American College of Physicians, they concluded that there was limited evidence showing acupuncture to be modestly effective for acute LBP.

In a recent meta-analysis of 11 RCTs with 707 patients with acute LBP, acupuncture was associated with modest improvements in the visual analog scale score, Oswestry disability score, and number of pills, but not the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire score. In another meta-analysis of 19 RCTs with 1427 participants with acute LBP, investigators also found all forms of acupuncture tested were effective in reducing pain (VAS score) compared to placebo or pharmacotherapy. Motion style acupuncture appeared to be the most effective treatment.

Authors of a cost-effectiveness analysis conducted in Norway with 171 participants with acute LBP concluded that a single treatment session of acupuncture in addition to usual care was cost-effective for quality-adjusted life years at one year but there was no significant difference in health care costs and societal costs at days 28 or 1 year.

There is moderate evidence that dry needling of myofascial trigger points, especially associated with other therapies, can reduce the intensity of low back pain, but safety, improvement of function and long-term effects are unclear.

Massage appears to be beneficial for patients with subacute and chronic back pain; good data on acute LBP are lacking. In the single trial on acute LBP included in this review, massage was superior to inactive controls for short-term pain, but not for function.
Monotherapy with traction is no more effective than sham, no treatment, or physical therapy.

Exercise therapy is as effective as either no treatment or other conservative therapies in decreasing pain and improving function in patients with acute LBP. In a recent meta-analysis of six trials with over 600 patients with uncomplicated sciatica, supervised structured exercise resulted in minimally less leg pain in the first 6 weeks, but overall was no better than generic advice to stay active. Authors of the most recent systematic review of 24 systematic reviews, including 21 RCTs of exercise for acute LBP, found no clinically important difference in pain or disability comparing exercise therapy to sham ultrasound, usual care, spinal manipulative therapy, advice to stay active, or education. NICE guidelines, however, endorse structured exercise programs.

Following lumbar disc surgery, exercise programs at 4 to 6 weeks postsurgery lead to a faster decrease in pain and disability vs. no treatment; study quality is low and effect size is small to medium. High-intensity vs. low-intensity exercise programs also lead to a slightly faster decrease in pain and disability but, again, study quality is low.

In a RCT of 220 adults with recent-onset LBP, early PT resulted in statistically significant but not clinically important improvement in disability. Early PT did not improve pain intensity or health care utilization compared with usual care at 4-week, 3-month, and 1-year follow-up. Authors of a cost-analysis of a single RCT found early PT to be cost effective for acute LBP but the magnitude of improvement in quality of life was small and probably not clinically meaningful.

In a recent RCT of 220 adult patients with sciatica of less than 90 days' duration, those referred for 4 weeks of physical therapy, including exercise and manual therapy, compared to education alone had greater improvement from baseline to 6 months in the Oswestry Disability Index (OSW) score and were more likely to self-report treatment success after 1 year (45.2% vs. 27.6% in the usual care/education group).

Authors of a systematic review of 11 clinical trials or cohort studies found that 5 of the 6 studies comparing early (within 30 days of LBP onset) vs. late PT reduced future health services utilization, including spine surgery; clinical trial data are needed.
The McKenzie method of PT is superior to other treatments with regard to short-term pain relief and disability, but these benefits are not evident in long-term followup.
Group formats for delivering PT appear to be equivalent to individual therapy for patients with LBP.

In a retrospective cohort study of 2184 patients with a new consultation for LBP, initiating PT within 14 days was not associated with LBP-related health care costs or utilization in the following year.
The addition of percutaneous radiofrequency treatment to physical therapy was no different from sham treatment plus physical therapy in a RCT of 60 patients with lumbar facet joint pain.

Posteroanterior mobilization at 3 cycles of 60 seconds applied at the L4 level in patients with LBP resulted in immediate and significant reduction in bending stiffness of the lumbar spine. Bending stiffness was highly correlated with pain magnitude both before and after mobilization.

Lumbar supports are of no benefit for treating LBP although a Cochrane review states findings are inconclusive. Non-rigid lumbar supports were found to be effective in reducing pain and disability in patients with non-specific LBP based on 4 trials; study quality was not reported.
Bracing (soft or rigid) did not improve pain or disability over no bracing for patients with osteoporotic compression fractures in one RCT.

Elastic taping does not appear to significantly reduce pain or disability immediately posttreatment for patients with specific or nonspecific spinal pain, myofascial pain syndrome, or whiplash-associated disorders.

There is moderate evidence that " Back schools ", in an occupational setting, reduce pain, and improve function and return-to-work status in the short and intermediate-term compared with other physical treatments or advise only.
There is no evidence that physical conditioning programs reduce sick leave in patients with acute LBP.
Bed rest in patients with uncomplicated LBP causes more pain and slows return to function. Similarly, patients with sciatica experience, at best, no benefit with bed rest.
Patients who were taught that they could function normally despite the presence of LBP returned to work faster than patients treated with usual care (58 days vs. 87 days).
The addition of motivational enhancement to physical therapy improved exercise compliance and showed trends in decreased pain and disability scores.

Authors of a Cochrane review of nine RCTs at high risk of bias, including 981 patients, found multidisciplinary biopsychosocial rehabilitation (therapy including a physical and psychological component) to be better than usual care for patients with subacute LBP. It was not clear if this treatment was better than other types of treatment.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found moderate to high-quality evidence that patient education increases reassurance, as measured by questionnaires of fear, worry, anxiety, and catastrophization, more than usual care/control education in the short and long term. Interventions delivered by physicians were significantly more effective than those delivered by other primary care practitioners. There was moderate-quality evidence that patient education reduces LBP-related primary care visits more than usual care/control education with a number needed to treat of 17 to prevent 1 LBP-related visit to primary care. However, in an RCT of 202 subjects with acute LBP, 2 one-hour educational sessions were no more effective than placebo education in improving pain outcomes.
Cognitive patient education intervention for LBP may be of some benefit, but study results have not reached statistical significance.
There is no evidence that TENS or behavioral therapy is more effective than other conservative treatments.
There is no comparative research on therapeutic ultrasound.

In a 4-arm RCT with 65 patients with acute LBP, low-level laser therapy plus drug therapy compared to drug therapy alone was more effective for pain relief and disability improvement; all groups improved from baseline.

Heat therapy is helpful in reducing pain and increasing function. In an RCT of 371 patients with nonspecific acute LBP, continuous low-level heat wrap therapy was superior to either acetaminophen or ibuprofen for early and extended pain relief, lateral trunk flexibility, early muscle stiffness and disability. There is no evidence that ice is beneficial.

Referral and prompt evaluation with appropriate imaging and other diagnostic studies are recommended in patients with the following: LBP unresponsive to conservative management for >4 weeks, severe or progressive neurologic deficit, or presence of "red flags" such as fever, nighttime pain, trauma, weight loss, age >50 years, history of cancer, or bladder or bowel incontinence.

Nonspecific acute LBP is a self-limiting condition, and most patients improve with or without treatment within 4 to 6 weeks.

A 3-item clinical prediction rule had poor to moderate discriminative performance for probability of sustained recovery from acute LBP (which occurred in 82%).The three items were: baseline pain (≤7/10 on a numerical pain rating scale), duration of current symptoms (≤5 days), number of previous episodes of LBP (≤1). Recovery for those with no predictors was slower, with about 70% achieving full recovery.
Psychological factors that predict poor outcomes include the presence of distress, depression, passive coping strategies, job dissatisfaction, disability claims, or somatization.

Authors of systematic review and meta-analysis found limited usefulness of 7 different screening instruments, including the STarT Back Tool and Orebro Musculoskeletal Pain Screening Questionnaire, for predicting pain outcomes, but 'acceptable' discriminatory ability for disability outcomes (AUC approximately 0.75).
In one study, the report of disability due to LPB was confounded by BMI, smoking and depression.

In a prospective cohort study of 115 patients seeking treatment for non-specific LBP in primary care, of whom 53.9% had an acute presentation, a persistent disabling condition and/or minimal important change in pain or disability occurred in 53.8% at 6 months. Factors associated with better outcomes for pain and disability were acute presentation (adjusted OR 0.34 and 0.26, respectively) and being employed (AOR 0.31; 95% CI, 0.11-0.92 for disability), while maladaptive psychosocial factors were significantly associated with poor outcomes for pain and disability (AOR 1.82 and 2.06, respectively).

Within the first month, patients typically experience rapid improvement (58% reduction of initial pain and disability scores). Additionally, among those who initially had to miss work, over 80% are able to return to work within 1 month.

In a systematic review of 11 prospective follow-up studies of at least 12 months, recovery from acute non-specific LBP was observed in only 33% of patients at 3 months and at one year 65% still reported pain. Complete pain absence at one year was present in only 29%.

In a metaanalysis of 15 studies of acute LBP, pain on a 100-point scale decreased from 69 at baseline to 28 at 6 weeks, 12 at 26 weeks, and 4 at 1 year. Disability scores were 57 at baseline, 28 at 6 weeks, 17 at 26 weeks, and 11 at 1 year.

Authors of a systematic review of clinical prediction rules found three that had undergone validation—the Cassandra rule for predicting long-term functional limitations and the five-item and two-item Flynn manipulation prediction rules for predicting a favorable functional prognosis in patients treated with lumbopelvic manipulation. There was no evidence, however, that using a prediction rule was of benefit on patient outcomes or improved resource use.

In one case series of 146 patients undergoing physical therapy, initial pain intensity and disability scores were the strongest predictors of 6-month clinical outcomes. Use of the STarT Back Screening Tool which includes psychological measure scores did not improve prediction of pain but added to the 6-month prediction of disability.

Authors of a systematic review including 25 articles, only one of which was rated as good quality and 19 studies rated as fair quality, concluded that higher pain intensity, higher body weight, carrying heavy loads at work, difficult working positions, and depression were the most frequently observed risk factors for LBP chronicity.

In a systematic review and prospective longitudinal study of patients following discectomy, recurrent back pain ranged from 3% to 34% at 6 to 24 months and 5% to 36% at >24 months; the frequency of same-level disc herniation requiring reoperation was 6%.
If the pain does not improve after 4 to 6 weeks of conservative therapy, labs (such as the erythrocyte sedimentation rate) or radiographs may be indicated.
If there are signs of radiculopathy after 4 to 6 weeks of conservative therapy, an MRI is recommended.
Any time the patient develops symptoms of cauda equina or severe or progressive neurologic deficit, an urgent consultation and MRI are recommended to evaluate for cord compression.
Intensive patient education is effective for patients with acute LBP; the value for patients with chronic low back pain is less certain.

In an Australian qualitative study of patient expectations of acute LBP management, most patients had a biomechanical understanding of back pain, expected X-rays to identify the cause of pain and knew how it should be treated, but had a poor understanding of its natural history. The doctor-patient relationship was important for patient satisfaction with care.
Acute nonspecific LBP has a good prognosis, although it appears that many patients continue to have some pain.
Patients should be encouraged to stay active; avoid aggravating factors, such as bending, twisting, or lifting; control pain; and prevent chronic pain.
Patients should be aware of "red flags" and advised to report their occurrence as soon as they develop.
Web information about LBP is often unreliable, especially that produced by for-profit entities. Only about 1 in 10 sites are of high quality.
The few studies on preventing and treating back pain in pregnancy are of limited quality and tend to be biased in favor of finding a benefit, so the data should be looked at with caution.
Low-moderate quality evidence supports land-based exercise for reductions in pregnancy-related LBP, disability, and sick leave more than usual prenatal care.
Water gymnastics appears to reduce LBP, and more women are able to continue to work.
Specially-shaped pillows help reduce pain in late pregnancy and improve sleep.
Both physiotherapy and acupuncture reduce LBP.

In an RCT of 400 women in their third trimester of pregnancy, women randomized to usual care plus OMT or usual care plus placebo ultrasound treatment compared to usual care only had significant reductions in pain and back-related functioning; the potential benefit of OMT in this population, however, remains unproven.
Pregnancy and lactation-associated osteoporosis (PLO) can lead to compression fractures and debilitating back pain. The incidence of PLO is low, but likely under reported.
In a metaanalysis of use of physical therapy for LBP in children and adolescents, combined physical conditioning and manual therapy was the most effective.

cell.label: Acute low back pain. Signs of cauda equina (saddle anesthesia, bowel or bladder dysfunction)?
Major cancer risk factors (new onset pain with history of cancer, multiple cancer risk factors, or strong clinical suspicion)?
Radiographs, sed rate initially, followed by MRI if indicated.
Other red flags (severe or persistent pain, significant neurologic deficit, significant trauma)?
Conservative therapy. Persistent radiculopathy in surgical or epidural injection candidate, or worsening symptoms or red flags at any time?
Continue conservative therapy. Consider physical therapy, massage, treatment for chronic back pain (see chapter).
